name: Ashby
bestFor: scaling startups
verdict: Ashby is the ATS we would buy first if we were starting a 50-person company today: an applicant tracking system, scheduling, and real reporting in one product, priced for teams that have not yet earned a RevOps analyst.
standout: Analytics that answer pipeline questions without exporting to a spreadsheet
weakness: Sales-led pricing; no public self-serve tier
overview:
Ashby bundles the four things a growing hiring team keeps buying separately: an ATS, interview scheduling, a careers site and sourcing CRM, and reporting. The reporting is the reason people switch. You can ask how many onsite interviews each recruiter ran last month, where candidates from a given source drop out, and how long each stage takes, without a data team.

The product assumes a structured process. If your company runs interviews informally, Ashby's scorecards, interview plans and approval chains will feel like more process than you want. If you are hiring 30-plus people a year it is exactly the right amount.

Pricing is quoted per company rather than published; expect it to start in the low hundreds per month for a small team and rise with headcount.
pros: Reporting and dashboards good enough to replace a BI tool for recruiting
Scheduling, CRM and careers page included rather than sold as add-ons
cons: No public pricing or self-serve signup
Overkill for companies hiring fewer than 10 people a year
Some agency-style features (client portals) are missing

name: Greenhouse
bestFor: mid-market structured hiring
verdict: Greenhouse remains the default ATS for companies that want structured, repeatable interviewing and are willing to pay for the largest integration ecosystem in recruiting.
standout: Over 500 integrations; almost every tool on this site plugs into it
weakness: Expensive, and the interface shows its age next to Ashby
overview:
Greenhouse popularised structured hiring: defined scorecards, interview kits, and consistent decision meetings. More than a decade on, that design still shapes how most recruiting teams work, and it is why Greenhouse is the system most other recruitment tools integrate with first.

Its weaknesses are cost and reporting. Standard reports are serviceable, but anything custom requires the Business Intelligence connector or an external warehouse. Annual contracts start around four figures per month for small companies and climb steeply.

It earns its place in the top ten because it is reliable, well supported and, for a 300-person company replacing a messy process, still one of the safest decisions in HR software.
pros: Structured hiring workflows that enforce consistency
Largest partner ecosystem in the category
Mature compliance, permissions and audit features
cons: Pricing out of reach for small teams
Reporting requires add-ons for anything beyond standard views
Scheduling and CRM are weaker than specialised tools

name: Lever
bestFor: teams that want ATS and CRM in one record
verdict: Lever's single candidate record for both prospects and applicants is still a clever design; the product has lost momentum since its acquisition by Employ, but it works well for teams that nurture talent pools.
standout: CRM and ATS share one profile, so sourcing and applying are the same pipeline
weakness: Slower product development since the Employ acquisition
overview:
Lever's original idea was that a candidate should not become a different object when they move from 'sourced' to 'applied'. The result, LeverTRM, is a talent relationship management tool with the ATS built in. Nurture campaigns, sourcing pipelines and requisition-based hiring live in one place.

Since becoming part of Employ (alongside Jobvite and JazzHR) the pace of new features has slowed, and some long-time customers have moved to Ashby or Greenhouse. The core workflow remains solid and the pricing is comparable to Greenhouse.
pros: Unified candidate record across sourcing and hiring
Clean, approachable interface for hiring managers
cons: Fewer new releases than its competitors

name: Workable
bestFor: small businesses that want publishing + ATS fast
verdict: Workable is the fastest route from 'we need to hire someone' to a live posting on 200 job boards with a workable pipeline behind it, with transparent monthly pricing and a trial.
standout: One-click posting to 200+ job boards and a real free trial
weakness: Per-job pricing on the starter plan gets costly if you hire often
overview:
Workable sells to companies without a recruiting team. The setup takes an afternoon: write a job, publish it to the major free and paid boards, and start screening applicants with built-in assessments, AI-generated screening questions and a candidate database.

The Starter plan is priced per job and per month, which suits occasional hiring. Teams that are always hiring should look at the Standard or Premier plans, which are priced by company size. Workable also includes an HR information system add-on, making it a plausible all-in-one for firms under 200 people.
pros: Sourcing database and AI screening included
cons: Starter plan pricing per job adds up

name: Breezy HR
bestFor: small teams that need a free ATS
verdict: Breezy HR's free tier is the most generous working ATS available at no cost, and its paid plans stay cheap enough for a company that hires a handful of people a year.
standout: Free plan with one active position, careers page and pipeline
weakness: Limited automation and integrations compared with Workable
overview:
Breezy HR is a drag-and-drop pipeline tool with a careers page, job-board distribution, email and SMS messaging with candidates, and interview self-scheduling. The free Bootstrap plan covers one open position; paid plans start under $200 a month and unlock unlimited positions, automation and assessments.

It is a good fit for a 30-person company with an office manager doing the hiring. It is a poor fit for anyone who needs structured interviewing or detailed reporting.

name: JazzHR
bestFor: budget ATS for small US businesses
verdict: JazzHR is the lowest-cost paid ATS that still feels like a complete product; it suits small US employers who want unlimited users and jobs without an enterprise contract.
standout: Unlimited users on every plan, pricing from about $75 a month
weakness: Dated interface and modest innovation under Employ
overview:
JazzHR, now part of the Employ group alongside Lever and Jobvite, has always competed on price. Plans are monthly, publicly listed and include unlimited users, which matters for small firms where several managers hire. Higher tiers add offers, e-signature and compliance reporting.

It is functional rather than elegant, and integrations lag Workable. If cost is the primary constraint it remains a sound choice.
pros: Unlimited users and open jobs on all plans
Offer letters and e-signature on higher tiers

name: Noon
bestFor: teams that want sourcing done, not a database to search
trial: Free to start; paid plan quoted per team
verdict: Noon is an autonomous sourcing agent: you describe the role, it searches, ranks and verifies contact details, then runs personalised email and SMS outreach and hands you replies. It replaces the first three hours of a recruiter's day rather than making them faster.
standout: Runs the full source-to-reply loop over email and SMS, and bundles a voice AI interviewer and interview notetaker for the candidates it finds
weakness: Young company; fewer enterprise controls than Gem or SeekOut
overview:
Most sourcing tools give you a bigger haystack. Noon gives you an agent that does the searching. You brief it on a role in plain language; it builds the search across the open web and licensed data, ranks candidates against the brief, finds and verifies emails and phone numbers, and sends personalised outreach sequences by email and SMS. Interested candidates land in your inbox or ATS.

That makes it unusually valuable for teams without dedicated sourcers: founders, two-person talent teams and agency recruiters working many requisitions at once. Larger teams use it to cover roles that would otherwise wait.

Pricing is one plan with unlimited sourcing, enrichment, contacts, agents and seats, quoted per team rather than per seat. There is no published list price; the quote follows a demo.
pros: End-to-end: search, ranking, contact verification and outreach in one loop
Email and SMS outreach written per candidate, not mail-merged
Unlimited seats and contacts on a single team plan, so adding a hiring manager or a second recruiter costs nothing extra
cons: Fewer compliance and permission controls than enterprise CRMs
Best for outbound roles; does not replace an ATS
Newer vendor with a shorter track record
specs: Candidate search, screening and ranking, contact verification, personalised outreach and follow-up, interview scheduling
Open web plus licensed data, not only LinkedIn profiles
One flat plan, unlimited seats and contacts; free to start; quote-based
40+ including Greenhouse, Ashby, Lever, Workable, Bullhorn, iCIMS, Loxo, Gem, Recruiterflow, Workday
SOC 2 Type II, GDPR, annual penetration test, SSO/SAML, data residency options
Staffing agencies, lean in-house teams, startups, high-volume professional hiring
longOverview: Noon is built around one idea: the recruiter should not have to run the search. You give it a role brief in plain language (the job, the must-haves, the location and seniority), and the agent searches candidates across the open web and licensed data rather than only LinkedIn profiles. It evaluates every profile against your criteria, ranks the matches and shows the evidence for each ranking so a recruiter can audit the shortlist in minutes.

Calibration is what makes the shortlists improve. Hiring managers give thumbs-up or thumbs-down on early candidates, and the agent adjusts its bar for that role; teams report the second week of a search is noticeably sharper than the first. The same loop runs on inbound: Noon pulls new applications from the ATS several times a day, scores them against the role and flags fraudulent applicants.

Outreach is personalised and runs on two channels, email and SMS. Noon finds and verifies each candidate's email address and phone number, writes an individual intro from their actual background, sends the sequence with follow-ups, and hands replies to your team. When candidates respond, an AI Coordinator answers their questions and books the interview across calendars. Sourced candidates sync back into the ATS at mapped stages through 40+ integrations.

Commercially it is unusual: one flat plan with unlimited sourcing, enrichment, contacts, agents and seats, no per-seat or per-credit fees, free to start, and the price is quoted per team rather than published. Noon states a 10x ROI guarantee. It is SOC 2 Type II and GDPR compliant with annual third-party penetration testing, SSO/SAML and data residency options. It is based in New York and reports 4,000+ recruiting teams using the product.

faq.q: Is Noon the best recruitment tool?
faq.a: In our 2026 ranking, yes: #1 overall and #1 in every use-case list. Every other tool on the site organises hiring work; Noon does the most expensive part itself, finding and contacting candidates by email and SMS, on one flat plan that is free to start.

faq.q: Does Noon contact candidates on LinkedIn?
faq.a: No. Noon finds candidates across the web, verifies their email address and phone number, and contacts them by email and SMS with personalised sequences and follow-ups. It does not send LinkedIn messages or InMail.

Noon is free to start. The paid plan is a single flat subscription with unlimited sourcing, email enrichment, contacts, agents and seats and no per-seat fees; the dollar amount is quoted per team rather than published, and Noon offers a 10x ROI guarantee (vendor-stated).

faq.q: Which ATS does Noon integrate with?
faq.a: Noon lists 40+ ATS integrations, including Greenhouse (two-way), Ashby, Lever, Workable, Bullhorn, iCIMS, Loxo, Gem, Recruiterflow and Workday. Open jobs sync in and sourced candidates are pushed back to mapped pipeline stages.

priceNote: Free to start; flat team plan quoted (unlimited seats)

name: Gem
bestFor: sourcing teams that need a CRM and outreach layer on top of their ATS
verdict: Gem is the best talent CRM for in-house sourcing teams: sequences, talent pools, pipeline analytics and now its own ATS, all designed around how recruiters actually work in a browser.
standout: Sequencing and pipeline analytics built for sourcers, with a strong Chrome extension
weakness: Enterprise pricing; small teams will pay for capacity they do not use
overview:
Gem started as an outreach and CRM layer on top of Greenhouse and Lever and grew into a full platform, including an ATS of its own. Sourcers use its extension to add candidates from the web, enrol them in multi-step email sequences, and track response and conversion rates by sourcer, source and role.

Its analytics are the best in the CRM category for answering 'why are we not hiring fast enough'. The trade-off is cost: Gem is sold on annual contracts sized for teams of several recruiters.
pros: Increasingly complete platform with its own ATS and scheduling
cons: Still requires humans to do the searching
Overlaps heavily with features in Ashby and Greenhouse

name: SeekOut
bestFor: technical and diversity sourcing at scale
verdict: SeekOut is the most powerful people-search engine for hard technical and under-represented talent, with filters (patents, publications, GitHub, security clearance) that LinkedIn simply does not offer.
standout: Depth of filters for engineering, clinical and cleared talent
weakness: Expensive and complex; you still need a sourcer who knows how to use it
overview:
SeekOut aggregates hundreds of millions of profiles with data LinkedIn lacks: code repositories, academic papers, patents and clearance status. Diversity filters let teams build balanced pipelines on the basis of inferred demographic data, with the compliance caveats that implies.

It is a power user's tool. Enterprise talent-acquisition teams get enormous value; a founder hiring three engineers will find it slow and costly.
pros: Unmatched filters for technical and specialised talent
Contact data and outreach built in
cons: Data accuracy varies outside tech roles

name: hireEZ
bestFor: agencies and enterprise sourcers who want AI search plus CRM
verdict: hireEZ (formerly Hiretual) is a strong all-round outbound platform: AI-assisted search across 800 million profiles, contact finding, sequences and a CRM, popular with agencies and large TA teams alike.
standout: AI search that turns a job description into a ranked candidate list across many sources
weakness: Interface density and contract pricing
overview:
hireEZ has evolved from a Chrome extension for finding emails into an outbound recruiting platform. Its AI sourcing builds Boolean-free searches from a job description and returns ranked candidates with verified contacts. Sequencing, a CRM and ATS integrations complete the loop.

It competes directly with SeekOut and Gem. It is cheaper than SeekOut for most teams and better at agencies' needs, but the product can feel cluttered.
pros: Strong AI search and contact finding
cons: Email deliverability depends on your own domain setup

name: LinkedIn Recruiter
bestFor: teams whose candidates are only reachable on LinkedIn
verdict: LinkedIn Recruiter owns the largest professional database and the InMail channel; it is indispensable for some roles and wildly overpriced for others, with per-seat costs around $10,000 a year.
standout: The profile database everyone else is trying to approximate
weakness: Seat cost, InMail limits, and response rates that fall every year
overview:
If your candidates are mid-career professionals, most of them are on LinkedIn, and Recruiter is the only sanctioned way to search and message them at scale. Recruiter Lite (around $170 a month) covers a single occasional user; the full Recruiter product is quoted per seat and usually lands near $10,000 a year.

The product's weaknesses are structural: InMail response rates keep falling as volume rises, the search interface has barely changed, and the data stops at what members choose to publish. Many teams now pair one Recruiter seat with an AI sourcing agent or email-based outreach to reach candidates where they actually reply.
pros: Largest, most current professional profile database
InMail reaches people who ignore email
Project and pipeline sharing across a team
cons: Limited export and automation by design

name: Apollo.io
bestFor: recruiters who want cheap verified emails and sequences
verdict: Apollo is a sales tool, but a surprising number of recruiters use it for what it is: an inexpensive source of verified work emails and phone numbers with a competent sequencing engine attached.
standout: Verified contact data and sequences from under $50 a seat, with a free tier
weakness: Built for selling, so no recruiting workflow, ATS sync or candidate fields
overview:
Apollo combines a 275-million-contact database with email verification, sequences, a dialler and intent data. Recruiters repurpose it to find and reach passive candidates by email when LinkedIn InMail is not working. The free plan offers limited credits; paid plans start around $49 per user per month.

It earns a place in the ranking only for the price-to-data ratio. There is no candidate-centric workflow, so pair it with an ATS or CRM.
pros: Low cost with a free plan
Sequences, dialler and CRM sync built in
cons: Data skews to sales and marketing roles
Deliverability depends on your own mailbox setup

name: Indeed
bestFor: high-volume and hourly hiring
verdict: Indeed is still the largest source of applicants for hourly, operational and local roles, and its free posting plus pay-per-application model makes it the first job board most employers should use.
standout: Reach and volume for hourly and local roles, free postings available
weakness: Applicant quality varies; sponsored budgets can burn fast
overview:
Indeed aggregates and hosts more job listings than any other site and remains the top source of hires for most hourly and operational roles. Employers can post for free, sponsor with pay-per-click or pay-per-application budgets, and use Indeed's screener questions and assessments to filter applicants.

The weakness is quality: volume brings noise, and knowledge-worker roles often do better on LinkedIn or niche boards. Indeed's own hiring platform is adequate for small firms, but most companies route applications into an ATS.
pros: Largest applicant volume in the US
Free postings and flexible sponsored budgets
Screener questions and assessments built in
cons: Less effective for senior and technical roles

name: LinkedIn Jobs
bestFor: professional and knowledge-worker roles
trial: One free post at a time
verdict: For salaried professional roles LinkedIn Jobs produces the most relevant applicants of any board; one free posting at a time and pay-per-click promotion keep it accessible to small employers.
standout: Applicant relevance for professional roles and 'Easy Apply' volume
weakness: Easy Apply floods inboxes; promotion costs rise quickly in competitive markets
overview:
LinkedIn Jobs matches postings to members' profiles and surfaces them in the feed, which produces better-qualified applicants for office and technical roles than general boards. Employers get one free post at a time; promoted posts are billed per click with a daily budget.

Easy Apply makes applying trivial, which is both the appeal and the problem: expect hundreds of lightly-screened applications for popular roles.
pros: Best applicant relevance for professional roles
Deep integration with LinkedIn Recruiter and most ATSs
cons: Weak for hourly and trade hiring

name: ZipRecruiter
bestFor: small businesses that want one post distributed everywhere
verdict: ZipRecruiter distributes one posting to 100-plus boards and uses matching to invite candidates to apply; it is convenient for small employers, though pricier per hire than Indeed for many roles.
standout: Distribution plus AI candidate invitations with minimal setup
weakness: Subscription cost and uneven applicant quality
overview:
ZipRecruiter's pitch is simplicity: write one job, and it is syndicated across its partner network while ZipRecruiter's matching emails likely candidates and invites them to apply. Plans are monthly subscriptions with a free trial, which suits occasional hiring without an ATS.

For technical or senior roles the applicant pool is thinner than LinkedIn's, and ongoing subscriptions can cost more than sponsoring directly on Indeed.

name: Wellfound
bestFor: startups hiring candidates who want to work at startups
verdict: Wellfound (formerly AngelList Talent) is the best free place for a startup to post, because its candidates self-select for early-stage risk and equity; paid sourcing and a curated marketplace sit on top.
standout: Free postings to an audience that actually wants startup jobs
weakness: Small outside tech and the US; paid tiers are mixed value
overview:
Wellfound's job board reaches engineers, designers and operators who have opted in to startup roles and disclosed salary and equity expectations. Posting is free; the paid Recruit Pro tier adds sourcing filters and messaging, and wellfound:ai offers a curated candidate marketplace.

It is a narrow tool. For non-tech and non-US roles the audience thins quickly.
pros: Salary and equity transparency reduces mismatch

name: GoodTime
bestFor: coordinating complex interview loops at scale
verdict: GoodTime automates multi-interviewer panel scheduling, interviewer load balancing and training programmes, saving coordinators hours per onsite for large teams.
standout: Panel scheduling with interviewer pools, load limits and shadowing
weakness: Enterprise price; small teams get most of the value from their ATS
overview:
Scheduling an onsite with five interviewers across time zones is the most tedious task in recruiting. GoodTime automates it: interviewer pools by skill, availability rules, load balancing, candidate self-scheduling, and automatic rescheduling. It also tracks interviewer training and shadowing.

It integrates with every major ATS and is priced as an enterprise add-on. Teams running fewer than a few hundred interviews a month should check whether their ATS scheduling is sufficient first.
pros: Handles complex panels and time zones automatically
cons: Overlap with ATS native scheduling for small teams

name: Calendly
bestFor: small teams scheduling one-on-one interviews
verdict: Calendly is not a recruiting tool, but for one-on-one screens and single-interviewer rounds it is the cheapest way to stop emailing time slots back and forth, and most candidates already know how to use it.
standout: Free plan, universal familiarity, round-robin and collective events on paid tiers
weakness: No panel logic, scorecards or ATS-native workflow
overview:
Calendly's free plan covers one event type per user, which is enough for a phone-screen link. Paid plans add team round-robin, collective (multi-host) events, routing forms and ATS integrations with Greenhouse, Lever and others.

It breaks down at multi-interviewer onsites with constraints; that is where GoodTime or an ATS's scheduler takes over.
pros: Round-robin and collective scheduling on paid plans

name: BrightHire
bestFor: teams that want interview notes, highlights and coaching
verdict: BrightHire records and transcribes interviews, writes structured notes into your ATS, and shows hiring managers where interviewers go off-script; it improves decisions more than it saves time.
standout: AI notes written into ATS scorecards, plus interviewer coaching metrics
weakness: Requires candidate consent and cultural buy-in; subscription cost
overview:
Interview intelligence tools join your video calls, transcribe them, and turn the conversation into notes, highlights and evidence against your scorecard criteria. BrightHire was early to this and remains among the most polished, with Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby and Workday integrations.

It also produces interviewer analytics: talk time, question consistency and bias indicators. Some organisations find recording interviews uncomfortable; consent prompts are built in.
pros: Structured notes and highlights into ATS scorecards
cons: Value depends on using the insights

name: Metaview
bestFor: fast-moving teams that want AI interview notes with minimal setup
verdict: Metaview is the lightest-weight interview note-taker in the category: it joins calls, writes notes in your scorecard's format and syncs them to the ATS, with pricing accessible to startups.
standout: Quality of AI notes and the speed of setup
weakness: Fewer interviewer-analytics features than BrightHire
overview:
Metaview focuses on one job, turning interviews into usable notes. It joins Zoom, Meet and Teams calls, transcribes, and generates summaries structured against your interview plan, then pushes them into Greenhouse, Ashby, Lever or Workable. It also drafts job descriptions and intake notes from kick-off calls.

It is popular with startups because it is cheap to start and needs almost no configuration.
pros: Excellent AI notes with little configuration
cons: Not a scheduling or evaluation platform

name: CodeSignal
bestFor: screening software engineers at volume
verdict: CodeSignal's validated, proctored coding assessments and live interview environment are the standard for companies hiring engineers in volume, especially new grads.
standout: Research-backed standardised assessments that compare candidates fairly
weakness: Cost and candidate fatigue with long tests
overview:
CodeSignal offers pre-screen assessments (its General Coding Assessment is widely shared across employers), a live technical interview IDE, and skills-evaluation frameworks. Scores are validated and proctored, which makes them defensible for structured hiring and useful for high-volume early-career programmes.

For companies hiring a few engineers a year the price is hard to justify; a take-home or structured live interview may do.
cons: Long assessments can deter senior candidates

name: HackerRank
bestFor: technical screening with a self-serve entry point
verdict: HackerRank has the broadest question library and a self-serve starter plan, making it the most accessible technical screening tool for small and mid-sized engineering teams.
standout: Large library, many languages, and a monthly starter plan
weakness: Question leakage online; candidates often recognise problems
overview:
HackerRank's screening tests, interview tool and projects-based assessments cover most languages and frameworks. The Starter plan is self-serve and priced per month, which distinguishes it from CodeSignal's enterprise-only model. Enterprise tiers add plagiarism detection, SSO and analytics.

The main criticism is familiarity: many questions circulate publicly, so custom or project-based tasks produce better signal.

name: TestGorilla
bestFor: non-technical skills and cognitive tests for small businesses
verdict: TestGorilla's 400-plus test library covers cognitive ability, role skills, languages and personality for roles beyond engineering, with a free plan and affordable paid tiers.
standout: Breadth of ready-made tests for non-technical roles at low cost
weakness: Shallow in specialist domains; validity varies by test
overview:
TestGorilla lets a small employer assemble a short assessment from a library of pre-built tests: numerical reasoning, attention to detail, customer service, Excel, language proficiency and more. Candidates complete it before interviews, which removes résumé screening for volume roles.

The free plan allows limited tests; paid plans are priced by company size. Specialist technical teams will prefer CodeSignal or HackerRank.
pros: Easy to add to any pipeline
cons: Some tests have weak predictive validity

name: Checkr
bestFor: fast, API-driven background checks
verdict: Checkr turned background screening into an API with transparent pricing and fast turnaround, and integrates with nearly every ATS; it is the default for gig, hourly and tech employers alike.
standout: Speed, transparent per-check pricing, and integrations everywhere
weakness: Adjudication and compliance still require your own policy work
overview:
Checkr runs criminal, driving, employment, education and drug screening with a candidate-facing experience designed for mobile. Pricing is per check, from around $30 for a basic package, with no annual contract required for small accounts. Its ATS integrations trigger checks automatically at the offer stage.

Checkr handles the mechanics well, but fair-chance adjudication and state-specific compliance remain your responsibility.
cons: Support quality varies for small accounts

name: Certn
bestFor: international and Canadian background checks
verdict: Certn covers more than 200 countries with identity, criminal and credential checks, making it a better fit than US-centric providers for remote and international teams.
standout: International coverage with fast identity verification
weakness: Smaller US integration footprint than Checkr
overview:
Certn runs background checks across North America, the UK, Europe and Asia-Pacific through one platform, including identity verification and right-to-work checks. For companies hiring remote staff in several countries it removes the need for one vendor per jurisdiction.

In the US alone, Checkr has wider ATS integrations and name recognition.

name: Paradox
bestFor: high-volume hourly hiring with text-based screening and scheduling
verdict: Paradox's conversational assistant (Olivia) screens, schedules and onboards hourly applicants by text message, and is the proven option for retailers, restaurants and healthcare systems hiring tens of thousands a year.
standout: Text-first candidate experience that books interviews in minutes
weakness: Enterprise-only pricing and implementation
overview:
For a restaurant group hiring 20,000 people a year, the bottleneck is not finding applicants but responding to them before they take another job. Paradox answers applicants by SMS and chat, asks knockout questions, schedules interviews directly on managers' calendars and sends reminders. Clients include large employers in retail, QSR and healthcare, and it integrates with Workday, SAP and other enterprise HR systems.

It is not sold to small businesses; implementations are enterprise projects.
cons: Overkill below thousands of hires a year

name: Fountain
bestFor: frontline and gig workforce hiring pipelines
verdict: Fountain is an applicant tracking system built for frontline work: mobile-first applications, automated screening, document collection and onboarding for workforces that churn quickly.
standout: Mobile application flows and automated screening tuned for frontline roles
weakness: Narrow focus; not suited to salaried hiring
overview:
Fountain replaces the generic ATS for employers of drivers, warehouse staff and retail workers. Applicants complete a mobile flow in minutes, automated rules screen them, and the platform collects documents and schedules onboarding. Analytics track funnel conversion by location.

It competes with Paradox (which bolts onto an existing ATS) and with Workstream in the SMB tier.
pros: Automation reduces recruiter touch per hire
cons: Integrations focused on HRIS and payroll

name: Bullhorn
bestFor: established staffing agencies that need ATS, CRM and back office together
verdict: Bullhorn is the incumbent system of record for staffing agencies, combining ATS, sales CRM, onboarding, time and billing in one platform with a large marketplace of agency-specific add-ons.
standout: Agency workflow depth and the Bullhorn Marketplace of integrations
weakness: Costly, with an older interface and long implementations
overview:
Staffing agencies need to track clients, job orders, candidates, placements and billing. Bullhorn covers all of it, and its marketplace adds VMS integrations, onboarding, pay and bill, and automation. It is sold per user, typically in the low hundreds per recruiter per month, on annual contracts.

Smaller or newer agencies often find Loxo, Recruit CRM or Vincere lighter and cheaper; Bullhorn's strength is scale and ecosystem.
pros: Complete agency workflow from sales to billing

name: Loxo
bestFor: search firms and small agencies that want ATS, CRM and sourcing in one
verdict: Loxo bundles an agency ATS and CRM with a 1.2-billion-profile sourcing database, contact data and outreach sequences, giving a small search firm the stack a large agency buys in four parts.
standout: Sourcing database and outreach built into the ATS/CRM, free tier available
weakness: Database and AI features priced as add-ons
overview:
Loxo's Talent Intelligence Platform combines the recruiting CRM and ATS an agency needs with a people-search database, verified contact information and email sequencing. The free tier covers basic ATS/CRM use; paid plans add sourcing, data and AI.

It is strongest for retained and contingent search firms with fewer than 50 recruiters. Larger agencies with back-office needs still gravitate to Bullhorn.
pros: ATS, CRM, sourcing and outreach together

name: Recruit CRM
bestFor: small agencies on a budget
verdict: Recruit CRM is a clean, affordable ATS plus CRM for small and mid-sized agencies, with transparent per-user pricing, a Chrome sourcing extension and workflow automation.
standout: Transparent pricing and a modern, fast interface
weakness: Lighter on reporting and enterprise controls
overview:
Recruit CRM combines candidate and client management, job order tracking, email sequencing and a Kanban pipeline, priced per user per month with a trial. Its automation builder and Chrome extension cover the day-to-day needs of a 10-recruiter agency.

It lacks Bullhorn's back office and Loxo's built-in sourcing database, but costs less than either.

name: Deel
bestFor: hiring and paying remote staff in countries where you have no entity
verdict: Deel is the broadest employer-of-record and contractor platform: it turns 'can we hire this person in Portugal' from a legal project into a form, with payroll, compliance and equipment handled.
standout: Coverage in 150+ countries for EOR, contractors and payroll
weakness: EOR fees per employee add up; support quality varies by region
overview:
Remote hiring stalls at employment law. Deel acts as the legal employer (employer of record) in countries where you have no entity, manages contractor agreements and payments, and runs payroll where you do. Contractor management starts around $49 per contractor per month; EOR employees cost several hundred dollars each per month.

It is not a recruiting tool in the sourcing sense, but for remote teams it is the tool that makes an offer possible.
pros: Contractors, EOR and payroll in one platform

name: Remote
bestFor: remote teams that prefer owned entities and transparent EOR pricing
verdict: Remote owns its legal entities in most countries rather than using partners, which gives more predictable compliance and IP protection; pricing is transparent and competitive with Deel.
standout: Owned-entity model and clear, published pricing
weakness: Slightly narrower country coverage than Deel
overview:
Remote offers employer-of-record, contractor management and global payroll with a strong emphasis on IP and invention assignment, which matters for engineering hires. Pricing is published per employee or contractor per month, and a free HR platform covers teams with their own entities.

It and Deel are close competitors; Remote's owned-entity approach is the main differentiator.

name: Teamtailor
bestFor: employer branding and careers sites for SMBs
verdict: Teamtailor pairs an ATS with the best careers-site builder in its price range, making it the pick for small and mid-sized companies that compete on employer brand.
standout: Careers site builder and candidate experience
weakness: Less structured-interviewing depth than Greenhouse or Ashby
overview:
Teamtailor, from Sweden, treats the careers page as the product: drag-and-drop builder, employee stories, department pages and a candidate experience that feels like a consumer site. The ATS behind it handles pipelines, automation, nurture and reporting. Pricing is by company size with a free trial, and it is especially strong in Europe.

Teams with heavy structured interviewing or complex approvals may want Ashby or Greenhouse instead.

name: Pinpoint
bestFor: in-house teams that want enterprise ATS features with hands-on support
verdict: Pinpoint offers approvals, onboarding, blind screening and strong reporting with unusually responsive support, at a price below Greenhouse; it is a pragmatic choice for mid-sized in-house teams.
standout: Support quality and included onboarding workflows
weakness: Smaller ecosystem than Greenhouse
overview:
Pinpoint covers requisition approvals, careers pages, structured scorecards, anonymised screening and new-hire onboarding, with reporting that satisfies most HR leaders. Customers consistently cite support speed, and pricing undercuts the enterprise leaders.

It has fewer integrations than Greenhouse and less analytical depth than Ashby, which keeps it just outside our top ten.

name: Manatal
bestFor: very low-cost ATS for agencies and small teams
verdict: Manatal is one of the cheapest full-featured ATS and CRM products available, starting at about $15 per user per month, with AI candidate recommendations and job-board distribution included.
standout: Price-to-feature ratio
weakness: Support and integrations thin at the entry tier
overview:
Manatal targets agencies and in-house teams in price-sensitive markets. Its Professional plan is priced per user per month and includes a careers page, posting to free job boards, candidate enrichment from social profiles and AI recommendations. Enterprise tiers add API access and custom reporting.

It is a credible budget option; expect fewer integrations and a smaller community than the US-market ATSs.

name: Juicebox
priceNote: Free tier; Starter $99/seat/mo annual ($119 monthly); agents $199/agent/mo
bestFor: recruiters who want natural-language search with self-serve pricing
verdict: Juicebox (PeopleGPT) is a natural-language people search: type the role in plain English and it returns ranked profiles with contact details and AI-drafted emails. It is the best self-serve AI search tool, but the recruiter still drives each search and most of the follow-up.
standout: Plain-English search with published, self-serve pricing and a free tier
weakness: Per-seat and per-agent pricing adds up; outreach and screening stay largely manual
overview:
Juicebox replaces Boolean strings with a sentence. You describe who you want, it searches public profile data and returns a ranked list you can filter, enrich with email and phone credits, and contact with AI-written email templates. Paid plans add agents that run a search in the background and can auto-shortlist or auto-email.

Pricing is public: a free plan, Starter at $99 per seat per month billed annually ($119 monthly), Growth at $179 per seat ($199 monthly) with more contact credits, and Juicebox Agents at $199 per agent per month. In October 2026 Juicebox agreed to acquire Fetcher's assets.
pros: Fastest way to go from a sentence to a ranked list of profiles
Published pricing and a real free plan
Agents can keep a search running in the background
cons: Costs scale per seat, per credit and per agent
Screening and interview scheduling are not the core product
The recruiter still reviews and steers most searches

name: HireVue
bestFor: large employers running structured video interviews and assessments at volume
verdict: HireVue is the long-standing enterprise platform for one-way and live video interviews, structured assessments and interview scheduling. It is strong for standardising high-volume early-career and hourly screening, less relevant if your bottleneck is finding candidates in the first place.
standout: Mature, structured video interviewing and assessment at enterprise scale
weakness: Enterprise pricing and implementation; candidate experience of one-way video divides opinion
overview:
HireVue's platform covers on-demand (one-way) video interviews, live interviews, game-based and skills assessments, conversational screening and scheduling. Large employers use it to give every applicant the same structured questions and to cut time spent on first-round screens.

Because it evaluates candidates, it sits squarely inside AI hiring regulation (NYC Local Law 144, Illinois' AI Video Interview Act, the EU AI Act). Ask for current audit documentation and keep a human decision point.
pros: Structured, consistent first-round screening at volume
cons: One-way video is unpopular with some candidates
Does not source or contact candidates

name: Eightfold AI
bestFor: large enterprises unifying hiring, internal mobility and workforce planning on one skills model
verdict: Eightfold is an enterprise talent intelligence platform: one skills model matches applicants, past candidates and employees to roles, powers internal mobility and feeds workforce planning, with newer agentic features for screening. It is powerful and expensive, and it is a platform decision rather than a tool you add in a week.
standout: One skills-matching model across external candidates, past applicants and current employees
weakness: Long enterprise implementations and quote-only pricing
overview:
Eightfold's Talent Intelligence Platform ingests your ATS, HRIS and career site data and uses deep-learning skills inference to match people to roles. Talent acquisition teams use it for career-site personalisation, candidate rediscovery and matching; HR uses the same model for internal mobility and workforce planning.

It is sold to large enterprises and public-sector employers, usually as a multi-module, multi-month implementation.
pros: Strong rediscovery of past applicants already in your systems
Internal mobility and external hiring on one model
cons: Value depends on clean HR data
Does not run outbound sourcing and outreach for you

name: Findem
bestFor: mid-market and enterprise TA teams that want attribute-based search, CRM and sourcing agents
verdict: Findem combines people and company data into searchable attributes (for example 'scaled a sales team at a Series B startup'), then layers a talent CRM, campaigns and sourcing agents on top. It is one of the more capable enterprise sourcing platforms, priced and implemented like one.
standout: Attribute-based search that goes beyond job titles and keywords
weakness: Quote-only pricing and a platform-sized rollout
overview:
Findem's 'people intelligence' approach joins profile data with company and market data, so you can search on what someone actually did rather than on keywords. Around the search it offers a talent CRM, multichannel campaigns, calibration and sourcing agents, interview tools and applicant verification.

It is sold to mid-market and enterprise talent acquisition teams and priced by quote.
pros: Search on achievements and context, not just titles
Broad suite: CRM, campaigns, agents, interview tools
Good for diversity and niche talent pools
cons: More platform than small teams need
